parts.title: Two Headlines
parts.text: On Monday, Cora noticed two headlines about the same vote on a new skate park. One read "Council Welcomes Park," the other "Council Gambles Budget on Teen Hangout." Dev, editor of the school news site, saw a lesson: the second headline tried to **sensationalize** a routine decision, making it sound far more dramatic. Yasmin added that the story felt **subjective**, shaped by opinions instead of facts.

parts.title: Looking Closer
parts.text: The friends made a checklist. First came **credibility**: who wrote the piece, and can its claims be checked? Next came the **framing**, the way word choices and angle shape how readers see a story. One article quoted only supporters, the other only neighbors worried about noise. Neither lied, yet each had an **omission**, a missing fact that changed the picture. Cora found a chart whose axis began at a high number, which would **distort** small differences into big ones. "That is **misleading**," Dev said, "even though every number is technically true."

parts.title: Their Own Standard
parts.text: Dev wanted their article to show strict **objectivity**, reporting facts without personal feelings steering. Yasmin warned that every writer has some **slant**, a leaning or point of view, so the goal was awareness. Their adviser said reporters should **disclose** any connections, since Cora's brother belonged to the skate club. They also vowed to avoid any **stereotype**, such as the idea that all teenagers cause trouble. When a classmate asked whether the principal could block the story, the adviser explained **censorship**, the official banning of material, noting that student reporters' rights vary.

parts.title: The Finished Story
parts.text: Their article gave both sides, listed every source, and ended with a note about Cora's brother. Readers wrote that it was less exciting but easier to trust. A good news story, Dev decided, is not a weapon or a show but a map, and readers deserve to see the whole territory.

definitions.meaning1: The quality of being believable and trustworthy. Example: The scientist's credibility grew after other labs confirmed her results.
definitions.studentChallenge: A source with no named author and no evidence has very little ___.

definitions.meaning1: The official banning or removal of speech, writing or art that someone in authority considers unacceptable. Example: The student newspaper protested the censorship of its editorial.
definitions.studentChallenge: Under strict ___, books and films had to be approved before anyone could see them.

definitions.meaning1: An oversimplified and often unfair idea about a group of people. Example: The film challenged the stereotype that scientists are always lonely and strange.
definitions.meaning2: To judge people according to such a fixed idea. Example: It is unfair to stereotype an entire group based on the behavior of one person.
definitions.studentChallenge: It is unfair to rely on a ___ instead of getting to know each person.

definitions.meaning1: A particular point of view, often one-sided. Example: The editorial had a clear slant in favor of a longer recess.
definitions.meaning2: To lean at an angle. Example: Late afternoon sunlight seemed to slant through the dusty window.
definitions.studentChallenge: The magazine's political ___ was obvious from the first paragraph.

definitions.meaning1: To reveal or make known information that was secret. Example: The mayor agreed to disclose the names of everyone who had donated to her campaign.
definitions.studentChallenge: Honest reviewers ___ it when a company gives them free products.

definitions.meaning1: To present information in a shocking or exaggerated way in order to attract attention. Example: Some websites sensationalize ordinary storms to win more clicks.
definitions.studentChallenge: A fair reporter will not ___ a small accident to make it sound like a catastrophe.

definitions.meaning1: The practice of judging or reporting on facts without letting personal feelings interfere. Example: A good referee must show objectivity, even when a friend is on the field.
definitions.studentChallenge: Reporters strive for ___ by keeping their personal feelings out of the facts.

definitions.meaning1: To twist something out of its true shape or meaning. Example: Statistics can distort the truth when key facts are left out.
definitions.meaning2: To change a sound or image so that it is unclear. Example: The old speaker would distort the music whenever the volume was too high.
definitions.studentChallenge: A funhouse mirror can ___ your reflection until you look tall and thin.

definitions.meaning1: Giving a wrong idea or impression, even without an outright lie. Example: The ad's tiny print made its low price misleading.
definitions.studentChallenge: A ___ map sent the hikers toward the wrong trail.

definitions.meaning1: Based on personal feelings, tastes or opinions rather than on facts. Example: Whether a song is good is subjective, since everyone's taste is different.
definitions.studentChallenge: A review full of personal feelings is more ___ than a list of measured facts.

definitions.meaning1: The way a story or issue is presented, including the angle, words and details chosen. Example: The framing of the headline made a small budget change sound like a disaster.
definitions.meaning2: The act of building the skeleton of a structure, or putting a frame around something. Example: Framing the walls of the new shed took the crew two days.
definitions.studentChallenge: The ___ of the report made the closing of the library sound like a victory.

definitions.meaning1: Something that has been left out. Example: The omission of one key fact changed the whole meaning of the report.
definitions.meaning2: An action that should have been done but was not. Example: Forgetting to lock the gate was a serious omission on his part.
definitions.studentChallenge: Leaving the date off the invitation was a costly ___.

His rules were simple. Reporters must _(9)_ any ties to advertisers. They should notice their own _(10)_ and avoid repeating any unfair _(11)_ about a group. And no one, he said, has the right to hide the truth through _(12)_.
